newsitem.title: FRANCE: Corsica separatist alleges secret talks with Paris.
newsitem.headline: Corsica separatist alleges secret talks with Paris.

text.p: A Corsican separatist chief living in hiding said in an interview on Monday that his group had held secret talks with the French government and he named five officials he called its envoys.
Francois Santoni, head of the Cuncolta Naziunalista party, said one of the envoys was Maurice Gourdault-Montagne, a senior aide of Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
Juppe's office dismissed Santoni's statements as "grotesque lies by a terrorist."
Santoni's party is the legal side of the outlawed Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC), "Historic Wing", the most hardline separatist group on the Mediterranean island.

Santoni also alleged in an interview with the daily Est-Republicain newspaper that a night-time rally in January of 600 heavily-armed FLNC guerrillas was organised at the behest of the government, which wanted to show the French public the group was popular in Corsica and should be negotiated with.
The rally caused uproar in France, especially since no one one was arrested even though police seemed to know about it.
Juppe's office said: "The government has but one policy in Corsica: development of the island, which relies on re-asserting order and thus strictly applying the laws as the population desires."
Newspapers have said the centre-right government has had contact with the guerrillas to try to find a negotiated solution to end a 20-year low-level bombing campaign on the island.
Justice Minister Jacques Toubon, in an interview with the daily Le Parisien out on Tuesday, said Santoni was on the list of wanted men. "Police are working to find him," Toubon said.

"People may have the impression that things are happening differently in Corsica, but that's not the case. You have to allow sufficient time for proceedings and we should have real results within a few months," he said.
Socialist party spokesman Francois Hollande said government contacts with the separatists were "an open secret" and authorities had fallen into "a trap of their own making."
"What is surprising in Santoni's interview is not so much what he said but that the press can go off and meet him when he is theoretically being tracked down by the police," he said.
The separatists maintained their bombings with an attack against the apartment of the mayor of the northern town of Bastia early on Monday.

The blast blew out the door of the home of Emile Zuccarelli, a former cabinet minister and opposition member of the National Assembly for the small Radical Socialist party. Zuccarelli was not at home and no one was hurt.

The FLNC claimed responsibility for the bombing and also said it was responsible for an attack in which the outside walls of an office of the paramilitary gendarmerie in Vescovato in northeastern Corsica were riddled with bullets on Monday.
In a statement sent to the media, the FLNC also claimed responsibility for 17 other attacks since September 5, including the bombing of the Bastia law courts, postal offices and banks.
